HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e114.summary: Title rubric for the second question of the Prologue: whether theology is a science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e121.summary: States the question: whether theology is a science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e128.summary: Principal argument that theology is not a science: what is not one science is not a science, since being and being one go together (Metaph. 4); but theology is not one science, since according to Averroes one science cannot treat equivocals, and things said of celestial and terrestrial bodies are said equivocally; creator and creature, which theology treats, are even more distant.
claims: What is not one science is not a science.
One science cannot treat equivocals.
Creator and creature are more distant than celestial and terrestrial bodies, so predicates of them are equivocal.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e171.summary: Argument to the contrary: a habit that considers a truly intelligible and supremely speculable subject under a determinate, special ratio is a specific habit, and theology is such (as shown in q.1). Thomas then divides the question into four articles: whether theology is a science; whether the articles of faith are its principles; whether it follows that it is a subalternate science; and whether it is properly called wisdom.
claims: Theology considers its subject under a determinate, special ratio and is therefore a specific habit.
The question has four articles: science, principles, subalternation, wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e193.summary: Beginning of the editorial 'Resolutio' (continued in the next paragraph): it is finally concluded that the theology of the wayfarer is a true science, but not...
claims: The theology of the wayfarer is a true science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e202.summary: Completion of the 'Resolutio': theology is a science not as the nature of the knowable object would allow but as the nature of the knower allows; its principles are the articles of faith; broadly speaking it is a subalternate science, and properly speaking it can be called wisdom.
claims: Theology is a science according to the capacity of the knower, not of the knowable object.
The articles of faith are its principles.
Theology is broadly a subalternate science and properly wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e220.summary: Opens Article 1 (whether theology is a science) by stating Thomas's position — theology is in some way a science, though not in the fully proper sense — and identifying two extreme contrary opinions: that it is a science properly speaking, and that it is in no way a science. He begins with arguments for the first opinion.
claims: Theology is in some way a science though not properly speaking.
Two extreme opinions oppose this: that it is science in the strict sense, and that it is no science at all.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e242.summary: First argument for theology being a science properly speaking: otherwise students would labor in it in vain.
claims: If theology were not a science, its students would labor in vain.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e254.summary: Second argument for the strict-science view: the only obstacle would be that God has no property really distinct from himself to be demonstrated of him; but metaphysics has being as subject, which has no properties really distinct from it (since what differs from being is nothing), and yet it has something functioning as a property. So too theology.
claims: Metaphysics demonstrates quasi-properties of being though none differ really from being; theology may do likewise for God.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e293.summary: Third argument for the strict-science view: the order between things really distinct remains where they are only conceptually distinct; substance, power and operation in creatures are essentially ordered so that one is demonstrated from another a priori, so in God too one may be demonstrated through another. Thomas rejects these arguments: strict scientific knowing (Post. An. 1) is knowing through the cause, but God and the divine have no cause; nor can theology know the cause through effects, since an effect yielding scientific knowledge of a cause must be adequate to it and no effect is adequate to God's power.
claims: Strict science is knowing a thing through its cause, and God has no cause.
Knowledge of God through effects is not strict science because no effect is adequate to the divine power.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e337.summary: Reply to the first argument: the student of theology acquires a most noble habit — noble not by scientific evidence but by the nobility of its subject — which can be called a science in some way, though not altogether properly.
claims: Theology's nobility derives from its subject, not from scientific evidence.
Study of theology is not vain, since it yields a habit that is in some way a science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e350.summary: Reply to the second argument: the lack of a distinct property is not the whole reason; theology is not a science in the strict sense because it neither reduces to self-evident principles nor presupposes them as evident in another science of which we are capable in this life.
claims: Theology is not strictly a science because it does not resolve into self-evident principles nor borrow them from a science accessible to wayfarers.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e366.summary: Reply to the third argument: as already said; alternatively, any complete demonstration about God would be formed in natural light and would therefore generate metaphysical rather than theological knowledge.
claims: A complete demonstration about God would proceed by natural light and thus be metaphysics, not theology.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e379.summary: Others argue for the strict-science view: the obscurity of faith is no more repugnant to science of credibles than the uncertainty of phantasms is to science of sensibles, yet we have science of sensibles despite uncertain phantasms.
claims: The obscurity of faith no more prevents science than the uncertainty of phantasms does.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e396.summary: Second argument of these others: the evidence of science is no more repugnant to the inevidence of faith than the clarity of knowledge of things in the Word is to the obscurity of knowledge of them in their own genus, and these coexist in the same intellect.
claims: Clear and obscure knowledge coexist in the same intellect (morning and evening knowledge), so faith and scientific evidence can coexist.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e409.summary: Further arguments of these others: God always provides his Church with perfect men able to defend the faith, which requires a scientific habit; and theology, as the noblest knowledge regulating all others, must be scientific. Since neither natural light nor the light of faith alone yields scientific evidence, they posit a special supernatural light — clearer than faith, dimmer than glory — granted to doctors of theology as perfected beyond the common state of the faithful; like dawn light, unlike noonday, it is compatible with the obscurity of faith. They cite Augustine on the two lights by which the uncreated light illumines the faithful: faith for infants, wisdom for the mature.
claims: The Church needs perfected men with a scientific habit to defend the faith.
There is a supernatural 'light of theology' between faith and glory granted to doctors of theology.
This intermediate light, like dawn, is compatible with the obscurity of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e465.summary: Thomas begins refuting the theory of a special light: a sign of knowing is the ability to teach (Metaph. 1), but no one can scientifically teach the content of faith to an unbeliever; nor does it help to say the unbeliever lacks the shared light, since no believer has ever been taught to know evidently what faith holds.
claims: The ability to teach is a sign of knowing, and no one can teach the faith scientifically.
No believer has been taught to know the articles of faith evidently.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e489.summary: Second refutation: the light of faith either remains in its perfect being with the special light, which is impossible (as extremes cannot coexist at their height, neither can an extreme with a mean), or is diminished, in which case the theologian would believe less and be less faithful than one without that light.
claims: The light of faith cannot coexist in full strength with a clearer light.
If faith is diminished by the special light, the theologian would be less faithful than others.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e509.summary: Third refutation: just as the light of glory, being clearest, wholly removes faith, so this greater light of understanding would at least diminish and obscure the light of faith.
claims: A greater light would at least dim the light of faith as glory removes it.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e522.summary: Fourth refutation: on their own account inevidence belongs to the ratio of faith, while the special light makes things evident; so the two are incompatible.
claims: Faith involves inevidence and the special light produces evidence, so they cannot coexist.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e534.summary: Fifth refutation: Aristotle argues against Plato that we cannot possess the noblest habits while they remain hidden from us; so too such a light could not be hidden from its possessor.
claims: The noblest habits cannot be hidden from those who have them.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e546.summary: Anticipated reply: Aristotle speaks of natural habits, whereas this light is supernaturally infused, and just as one in charity does not know he is in charity, so with this light.
claims: Supernaturally infused habits, like charity, can be hidden from their possessor.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e559.summary: Rejoinder: a light that causes scientific evidence manifests itself and cannot be hidden from its possessor, whereas charity is not a cognitive habit and therefore can be.
claims: A light producing scientific evidence is self-manifesting.
Charity, being non-cognitive, can be hidden from its possessor.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e572.summary: Further refutation: as one natural light suffices for all naturally knowable things, so the single supernatural light of faith suffices for all supernatural things knowable in this life.
claims: The light of faith suffices for all supernatural knowledge available in the present life.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e585.summary: Further refutation: the posited mean light between glory and faith is either a mean by participation (mixing both extremes, so faith would not remain in its proper nature, as in mixed colors) or a mean by negation of both extremes (which would exclude faith and could be infused into an unbeliever). Thomas then begins replying to the motives: to the first, the minor is false, since every science requires certain phantasms.
claims: A mean by participation would compromise faith's proper nature.
A mean by negation would exclude faith altogether.
Every science requires certain phantasms.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e620.summary: Objection and replies: we have certain science of the sun's size exceeding the earth, though its phantasm is uncertain; Thomas answers that uncertain phantasms are resolved into certain ones, as astronomers through geometry and perspective learned how apparent size decreases with distance. Reply to the second motive: inevidence and evidence about the same object are more repugnant than clarity and obscurity about different objects; knowledge in the Word has the divine essence as principal object, whereas faith and the supposed light concern the same object. Reply to the third: defenders of the faith need no special light; it suffices that they be trained in theology with divine grace cooperating.
claims: Uncertain phantasms yield science only by resolution into certain ones.
Evidence and inevidence about the same object are incompatible, unlike clarity and obscurity about different objects.
Defenders of the faith need only theological training and grace, not a special light.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e676.summary: Reply to the fourth motive: theology can be noblest by the nobility of the light of faith and of its object without being simply scientific.
claims: Theology's nobility derives from faith and its object, not from strict scientific character.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e687.summary: Thomas charges the proponents of the special light with a fallacy of the consequent: it does not follow that if theology is a science it is so by such a light, since many hold it to be a science properly speaking without positing that light.
claims: Theology's being a science does not entail a special light.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e714.summary: Their examples tell against them: darkness is privation of light and is compatible with no degree of light; so if obscurity belongs to the formal ratio of faith, faith cannot coexist with any evidence-making light.
claims: If obscurity is essential to faith, faith cannot coexist with any evidence-producing light.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e725.summary: Qualification: Thomas does not deny that the heavenly Consoler refreshes his devout with various revelations and secrets, but this is by special grace and a singular privilege, which does not establish a common law. He denies the special light for doctors of theology as a state, not for the singularly devout — otherwise he would contradict the Augustine prayer cited in his principium. This also answers the Augustine authority.
claims: Special revelations to the devout exist by singular grace but do not constitute a common state of theologians.
A singular privilege does not establish a common law.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e754.summary: Another group holding theology to be a strict science claims it proceeds from self-evident common conceptions, not articles of faith, because posterior things are proved by prior ones, and what theology considers is, for our intellect, posterior to what metaphysics considers, since being as being is prior to God and every determinate being.
claims: Theology proceeds from self-evident common conceptions rather than articles of faith.
Being as being is prior for our intellect to God, so theology can be proved from metaphysical principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e776.summary: Further arguments of this group: natural light teaches that every perfect operation terminates in a product; we know naturally that God understands and wills perfectly; so there are two divine products, Word and Love, i.e., Son and Holy Spirit. Others argue that the power of the cause is preserved in the effect, so a conclusion drawn from one naturally known and one believed premise is in some way naturally known (e.g., every man has true flesh; the Son of God is man; so the Son has true flesh).
claims: The Trinity of processions can be derived from natural knowledge of divine understanding and willing.
A conclusion from a naturally known and a believed premise retains some natural knowledge.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e810.summary: Thomas judges this view worse than the others, since it would annul the merit of faith — faith has no merit when human reason provides proof (Gregory).
claims: Deriving the articles from natural reason would nullify the merit of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e821.summary: Reply to the first argument: from universal, higher terms one can conclude what is common to inferiors, but not what is proper to them; taken indefinitely the higher term does not infer the lower, taken universally the proposition is false. Through 'being' one can prove that God is good or other common predicates, but not that he is Father or Son.
claims: Universal terms yield only common predicates of inferiors, not proper ones.
From 'being' one can prove common predicates of God but not the personal properties of the Trinity.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e847.summary: Reply to the second argument: the major holds of transitive, not immanent, operations like understanding and willing; moreover, since in God understanding and willing are really identical (as both theologians and philosophers attest), arguing from distinct operations to distinct products would yield only one product, which is heretical.
claims: Not every perfect immanent operation yields a product.
Since understanding and willing are identical in God, the argument would yield only one procession, which is heretical.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e867.summary: Reply to the third argument: just as from a necessary and a contingent premise follows a wholly contingent conclusion (Prior Analytics 1), so from a naturally known and a believed premise follows a conclusion wholly believed and in no way naturally known — as a necessary cause acting through a contingent cause produces a wholly contingent effect.
claims: A conclusion from a known and a believed premise is wholly believed.
The conclusion follows the weaker premise.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e891.summary: Thomas turns to the opposite extreme, that theology is in no way a science, which he dismisses as erroneous for lack of weighty arguments and as condemned in the Paris articles of 1277 ('that one knows nothing more by knowing theology'). He introduces two related opinions, the first holding that theology knows only consequences (inferential connections), not consequents or conclusions: e.g., the theologian knows that if there are three persons in one nature, their distinction is by relations, without knowing antecedent or consequent.
claims: The view that theology is no science at all is erroneous and condemned in the Parisian articles.
Some hold that theology is a science only of consequences, not of conclusions.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e942.summary: Refutation of the 'science of consequences' view: it too falls under the condemned article, since knowledge of a consequence taken formally, abstracting from knowledge of antecedent and consequent, is purely logical and obtainable from logic alone; so nothing more would be known by knowing theology.
claims: Knowledge of consequences abstracted from their terms is purely logical.
On this view theology would add nothing beyond logic, contrary to the condemned article.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e962.summary: Second refutation: on that view theological knowledge would be no truer than knowledge of fictions, since one knows 'a chimera is God, so a chimera is omnipotent' to be a valid consequence while ignoring both terms. Knowledge of consequences so taken is purely logical, because ignorance of logic alone causes ignorance of consequences (per Averroes), so knowledge of logic alone causes their knowledge.
claims: Theological knowledge of mere consequences would be no truer than knowledge of fictions.
Knowledge of formal consequences is caused solely by logic.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1001.summary: Anticipated reply: the argument holds for a consequence in itself but not as taken in determinate subject matter.
claims: Consequences in determinate matter may not be purely logical.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1012.summary: Rejoinder: since the opponent takes the consequence formally, abstracting from certain knowledge of antecedent and consequent, the matter cannot help; knowledge of it will always remain purely logical.
claims: A consequence taken formally yields only logical knowledge regardless of its matter.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1028.summary: Third refutation: as judging whether a construction is grammatical in any science belongs to grammar alone, so knowing whether a consequence is necessary in any matter belongs to logic alone, while knowing the conclusion inferred belongs to the particular sciences.
claims: Validity of consequences belongs to logic, knowledge of conclusions to particular sciences.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1050.summary: A second related opinion grants nothing to the wayfarer's theology: theology in itself is a most evident science of supremely true things, but for us it is not a science, owing not to its content but to our deficiency (the owl's eye before the sun). They add that broadly, as science is had insofar as the nature of the matter allows in the present state, theology may be called a science, as moral science gives only figural knowledge. Thomas argues they contradict themselves: if the matter is supremely knowable and we have science as the nature of the thing allows, our theology would be science properly speaking.
claims: Some say theology is a science in itself but not for us.
This view is internally inconsistent: if knowledge accords with the nature of a supremely knowable object, it would be strict science.
concepts: theologia in se vs quoad nos

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1114.summary: Another opinion distinguishes three theological habits: one by which the contents of Scripture are known, which is faith and only very broadly science; a 'defensive' theology that declares and defends the faith (Augustine, De Trin. 14); and an 'elicitive' theology deducing conclusions from the articles. They hold that neither of the latter two is a science, either because no demonstration is possible about its matter or because wayfarers cannot demonstrate it.
claims: Theology may be divided into contentive (faith), defensive and elicitive habits.
Neither defensive nor elicitive theology is a science for the wayfarer.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1162.summary: Refutation of the three-habit view: by the same reasoning every science, such as metaphysics or logic, would have contentive, defensive and elicitive habits. The distinction also collapses: the Old and New Testaments explain and defend each other (against Jews and heretics), so contentive and defensive coincide; and the theologian rarely elicits a conclusion except by declaring, so defensive and elicitive coincide.
claims: The three-habit division would apply equally to every science.
The members of the division coincide and so do not constitute distinct habits.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1204.summary: Thomas's own conclusion: the theology of the wayfarer is truly a science, not as the nature of the knowable thing permits but as the nature of the knower permits. A habit that proves something of its subject by reasoning no less infallible than economics or politics proves of theirs is truly scientific; theology does so, e.g., by the syllogism: whatever has the ratio of ultimate end is the highest good and can satisfy all the soul's desire; God as glorifier has the ratio of ultimate end; therefore God is supremely good and can beatifically satisfy the soul. The minor is evident since 'glorifier' expresses the subject in relation to the end (q.1). Thus theology proves quasi-properties of its subject as effectively as moral science.
claims: The wayfarer's theology is truly a science according to the knower's capacity.
Theology proves properties of its subject with no less certainty than economics or politics.
God as glorifier has the ratio of ultimate end and can therefore beatify the soul.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1267.summary: Anticipated objection: theological teachings are not shown demonstratively, and since demonstration is a syllogism producing knowledge, theology is not a science.
claims: Without demonstration there is no science, and theology lacks demonstration.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1280.summary: Reply: if 'demonstration' means demonstratio potissima, only mathematics would be a science, being alone in the first degree of certainty (Averroes); if it means an efficaciously concluding syllogism, even from suppositions rather than first principles, then theological reasons are demonstrations. A further objection is raised: such syllogisms are not found everywhere in theology.
claims: Only mathematics has demonstratio potissima.
Theology has demonstrations in the sense of efficaciously concluding syllogisms from suppositions.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1311.summary: Reply to the further objection: neither are they in other sciences; in logic, natural philosophy, metaphysics or any other, for every efficacious argument there are a thousand words false, useless or inconclusive, and the so-called strict sciences rarely demonstrate anything potissime.
claims: Strict demonstrations are rare in all sciences, not only theology.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1334.summary: Continues: the rarity of demonstration in the philosophical sciences is shown by the pervasive disagreement in them, so that we seem to have opinion more than science in philosophy, or at least no less science in theology than in philosophy. No one knows definitively the quiddity even of an ant, since philosophers describe substantial differences through accidents; we do not even know ourselves — Averroes held a single intellect for all, others transmigration or a corruptible intellectual soul; among Christians, England holds plurality of substantial forms while Paris condemns it, and opinions vary on whether the soul's powers are identical with its essence. Second argument: a habit that sufficiently solves all objections against its truths is scientific (Metaph. 3), and theology does so. He then presents three objections to this claim: solving all objections against the Trinity would show it not impossible, hence possible, hence (among eternal things) necessary and demonstrable; what cannot be sufficiently proved cannot have its opposite sufficiently disproved; and solution by interemptio requires an instance outside the case.
claims: Philosophical sciences are riddled with disagreement and rarely attain strict knowledge.
We do not know the quiddity even of an ant or of our own soul.
A habit that can sufficiently solve all objections against its truths is scientific, and theology can do so.
Objectors argue that sufficiently solving objections to the Trinity would amount to demonstrating it.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1467.summary: Third objection: if one solves by interemptio (denying a premise), one must give an instance outside the case at hand; but nowhere in nature except the divine nature are three supposits found in one undivided essence, so no counter-instance against an argument against the Trinity can be given.
claims: Refutation by denial requires a counter-instance, and the Trinity has no natural analogue.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1491.summary: Thomas explains how objections against the faith are solved: as fallacies are in dictione or extra dictionem, so solutions are by distinction (identifying a formal fault) or by interemptio (identifying a material fault). Since all arguments against the Catholic faith are false sophisms (Augustine, City of God; Letter to Marcellinus), all can be solved one of these ways. Example: an unbeliever argues that supposits cannot be multiplied without multiplying the nature; Thomas distinguishes absolute from relative supposits — the major holds of absolute supposits, the minor of relative ones, and nothing prevents three persons in one nature distinguished by opposed relations.
claims: All arguments against the faith are sophisms and can be solved by distinction or by interemptio.
Three divine persons can be in one nature because they are relative, not absolute, supposits distinguished by opposed relations.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1563.summary: Anticipated rejoinder of an unbeliever: the solution assumes something false, since opposed real relations cannot exist together in the same undistinguished foundation.
claims: Opposed real relations cannot coexist in one undistinguished foundation.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1574.summary: Reply: distinguish a finite from an infinite foundation — the claim holds of a finite foundation but not of an infinite one. Some add that opposed relations can coexist in one foundation, as mover and moved when something moves itself.
claims: Opposed relations cannot share a finite foundation but can share an infinite one.
Self-motion shows opposed relations in one foundation.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1594.summary: Further rejoinder of the unbeliever: relative supposits cannot be in an absolute nature. Thomas responds by interemptio, giving the reason for denial: whoever judges of something exceeding his intellect and mode of consideration judges rashly, and how three relative supposits are in one infinite divine nature exceeds the intellect of any worldly philosopher.
claims: One who judges matters exceeding his understanding judges rashly.
How three relative supposits exist in one infinite nature exceeds philosophical understanding.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1619.summary: Continues the reply: just as Aristotle, even as metaphysician (Metaph. 12), refused to judge presumptuously of the exact number of intelligences and deferred to a higher inquiry, so much more must the philosopher defer to a higher authority on the articles of faith.
claims: The philosopher must defer to a higher authority on the articles of faith, as Aristotle deferred on the number of intelligences.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1637.summary: Reply to the first objection (solving objections would demonstrate the Trinity): the theologian's solution does not show the article to be not impossible; it shows the philosopher that his middle term is extraneous and inapplicable to the conclusion he seeks to refute, since that conclusion exceeds his entire faculty. Even if, per impossibile, the philosopher's anti-faith conclusion were true, it would still be shown that his middle term is impertinent and does not conclude.
claims: Solving objections to the faith shows the opponent's middle term to be irrelevant, not that the article is possible or necessary.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1668.summary: Reply to the second objection: faithful solutions do not directly disprove the opposite of the faith but show that unbelievers' reasons do not conclude. Reply to the third: an instance outside the case is needed only when no reason for the denial is given; when it is, an instance within the case suffices. Whether some articles, like temporal creation, can be proved by efficacious reason is deferred to Book 2. Thomas closes Article 1 with authorities supporting his conclusion: Paul's calling theology science and wisdom; Augustine's 'science of salvation' and 'science of faith'; Richard of St. Victor's aim to find necessary reasons; and Anselm on the Proslogion and Monologion proving by necessary reasons what faith holds.
claims: Solving objections shows only that unbelievers' arguments fail, not a direct disproof.
When the reason for a denial is given, an instance within the case suffices.
Scripture and the Fathers call theology a science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1744.summary: Article heading and question: whether the articles of faith are the principles of the science of theology.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1753.summary: Thomas briefly answers Article 2 affirmatively: the articles of faith are the principles of theology, since by reference to them everything considered in theology is regulated and directed. Some argue otherwise in many ways.
claims: The articles of faith are the principles of theology because everything in theology is regulated by them.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1769.summary: First two arguments against the articles as principles: no science proves its principles but presupposes them, yet all theology is ordered against heretics and unbelievers who deny the articles; and no science inquires into or concludes its principles, yet theologians form and conclude questions about the articles in almost all their books.
claims: No science proves or inquires into its own principles.
Theology proves and inquires into the articles against heretics, so they are not its principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1790.summary: Third argument: in no science are principles less known than conclusions (Post. An. 1), but the articles are only believed while theological conclusions are in some way known (Article 1).
claims: Principles cannot be less known than conclusions, yet articles are merely believed while conclusions are known.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1806.summary: Fourth argument: 1 Peter 3:15 says those with theology must always be ready to give a reason for the faith that is in us.
claims: Theologians must give reasons for the faith, implying the articles are proved.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1817.summary: Fifth argument: Augustine ordered all of De Trinitate to declaring the article that God is triune and one, and says all earlier Catholic expositors aimed to teach from Scripture that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are of one substance.
claims: Augustine's De Trinitate aims to declare an article of faith, so theology declares the articles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1842.summary: Further authority: Augustine (De Trin. 14) says theology includes only what generates, nourishes, defends and strengthens saving faith. Hence the articles are defended and declared by theology and cannot be its principles, since a science does not prove its principles (Physics 1; Post. An. 1).
claims: Theology defends and declares the articles, and a science does not prove its own principles, so the articles are not principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1881.summary: Reply to the first argument: the major is false, since metaphysics (Metaph. 4) proves its own principles.
claims: Metaphysics proves its own principles, so not every science merely presupposes its principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1892.summary: Anticipated objection: this is irrelevant, since metaphysics is a common science while theology is special, so what holds of metaphysics need not hold of theology.
claims: A common science may prove its principles, a special one cannot.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1904.summary: Reply: the opponents took the major absolutely and universally ('no science proves its principles'), so a single counter-instance suffices to refute it.
claims: A universal negative is refuted by one counter-instance.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1924.summary: Some doctors answer differently: principles can be proved explicitly (as metaphysics does) or implicitly; every special science implicitly proves its principles, since destroying the conclusion destroys a premise and ultimately a principle, so whoever explicitly defends a conclusion implicitly defends its principles.
claims: Every special science implicitly proves and defends its principles by defending its conclusions.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1961.summary: Thomas rejects this: though from the falsity of a conclusion one may infer falsity in a premise, from the truth of a conclusion one cannot infer the truth of the premises, since truth can follow from falsehood (Prior Analytics 2).
claims: The truth of a conclusion does not establish the truth of its premises.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e1977.summary: Note: though theology is the most special science by reason of its subject — which is not merely specifically but numerically one — it is the most common by reason of what it considers, treating God and every creature as leading to the creator and the ultimate end. So even if theology as a special science cannot prove its principles, as a common science it can prove and declare them.
claims: Theology is most special in subject (numerically one) and most common in scope.
As a common science theology can prove and declare its principles.
concepts: theology as special and common science

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2008.summary: Reply to the second argument: one may inquire about something either because it is doubted (as in Topics 1), which does not occur with principles, or because its application in special matter is doubted. In the latter sense questions must be raised about principles, lest heretics, presupposing them, make false applications by pseudographic syllogisms. Theology inquires into the articles only in this second way.
claims: Principles are not doubted, but their application to special matter may be.
Theology raises questions about the articles to prevent heretics' false applications.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2045.summary: Reply to the third argument: the major is false for every subalternate science, which presupposes its principles as evident in a higher science; and theology resembles subalternate sciences (see Article 3).
claims: In subalternate sciences principles may be less evident to the knower than conclusions.
Theology resembles a subalternate science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2062.summary: Reply to the authorities: they are answered by what was said. To Peter's 'giving a reason', we give reasons for the articles by answering the opposing arguments in the manner described above.
claims: Giving a reason for the faith means answering objections, not demonstrating the articles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2075.summary: Thomas proves his thesis that the articles are theology's principles. First argument: principles are those to which other things are judged truer the more they conform, since principles are the rule and measure of all else in a science; and in theology each thing is reckoned truer the more it conforms to the articles, while whatever dissents from them is rejected as error.
claims: Principles are the rule and measure of truth within a science.
In theology things are judged true by conformity to the articles of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2112.summary: Second argument: in every art the propositions we most firmly adhere to, and for whose sake we adhere to the conclusions, are its principles (Post. An. 1); in Scripture we adhere most to the articles of faith and to everything else because of them.
claims: The propositions we adhere to most, and for whose sake we accept others, are a science's principles.
In theology these are the articles of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2130.summary: Third argument: propositions formed about a science's subject that cannot be proved by anything prior in that science are its first principles; the articles are such in theology.
claims: The articles cannot be proved by anything prior within theology and so are its first principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2146.summary: Anticipated objection: even if not proved by prior things, the articles can at least be declared and proved by posterior things.
claims: The articles can be proved a posteriori.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2155.summary: Reply: this does not undermine their being principles, since even the first principle (Metaph. 4) is proved and declared a posteriori. Fourth argument: what a science presupposes as most true are its principles (Post. An. 1), and theology so presupposes the articles.
claims: Even the first principle of metaphysics is declared a posteriori, so a posteriori declaration does not undermine principle status.
What a science presupposes as most true are its principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2178.summary: Article heading and question: whether theology is a subalternate science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2201.summary: Thomas answers Article 3: broadly speaking theology can be called subalternate, since it does not reduce to self-evident principles but presupposes its principles as most known in the science of God and the blessed, which God can reveal when he wills. Properly it is not subalternate, since anyone with a subalternate science can naturally attain the subalternating science in which its principles are evident, whereas the theologian cannot naturally attain the science of God and the blessed. This distinction reconciles the two opinions — one affirming, one denying subalternation — as Giles of Rome showed in his commentary on the Prologue.
claims: Theology is broadly subalternate to the science of God and the blessed.
Properly it is not subalternate, because the theologian cannot naturally attain the subalternating science.
The distinction reconciles the opposing opinions, following Giles of Rome.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2253.summary: Introduces another doctor who directly opposes this: he holds that a subalternate science does not depend on the subalternating science by receiving its principles from it as manifesting their cause, which he proves in three ways.
claims: A subalternate science does not receive its principles from the subalternating science as manifesting their cause.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2269.summary: The doctor's first proof: otherwise the subalternate science would act beyond its species, since every science's consideration stops at its principles; if through the subalternating science it knew their cause, its consideration would not stop at its principles.
claims: A science's consideration terminates at its principles, so knowing their cause would exceed its species.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2288.summary: Second proof: otherwise a subalternate science could demonstrate its principles, since whoever knows the cause of something can demonstrate it through that cause; but this is repugnant to every science.
claims: Knowing the cause of one's principles would allow demonstrating them, which no science does.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2301.summary: Third proof: otherwise no one could learn a subalternate science without the subalternating one, since knowledge of conclusions presupposes knowledge of principles; but the principles of subalternate sciences can be known through sense, memory and experience (Post. An. 2) without prior knowledge of the higher science.
claims: Subalternate sciences can be learned without the subalternating science, as their principles are known by experience.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2336.summary: Thomas argues that this doctor soon contradicts himself: he says our theology, though not properly subalternate, depends on God's science for its certainty as a disciple depends on a teacher (citing Aristotle on the learner believing and Augustine on believing those who see invisibles), and that this is a subordination resembling subalternation. But if theology resembles subalternate science in this, then properly subalternate sciences must have evident certainty of their principles only from the subalternating science — as a meadow 'laughs' by likeness to man, where laughing belongs properly to man.
claims: The opposing doctor admits theology depends on God's science as a learner on a teacher.
If theology resembles subalternation in this respect, the feature must belong properly to subalternate sciences.
What belongs to something by likeness belongs properly to its analogue.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2404.summary: Reply to the first proof: though not by its own power, a science can act beyond its species by a superior's power, as heat, an accident, produces fire by the power of fire's substantial form; so a subalternate science, with the subalternating science cooperating, can grasp the cause of its principles. Of itself its consideration stops at principles, but by another's power it can transcend them.
claims: A subalternate science can, by the power of the subalternating science, know the cause of its principles.
Of itself a science stops at its principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2428.summary: Reply to the second proof: as subalternate, a science does not demonstrate its principles; but as the natural philosopher who 'puts on' the habit of the metaphysician proves his principles, so one with a subalternate science who puts on the subalternating habit can declare its principles.
claims: One possessing both sciences can declare the lower science's principles by means of the higher.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2447.summary: Reply to the third proof: a subalternate science remaining wholly within its own power and limits can be learned without the subalternating science, since it suffices to presuppose its principles as known by the truth and evidence of the higher science; but with the help of the higher science it can know or understand its principles in the way described.
claims: A subalternate science can be learned alone by presupposing its principles, but knows them evidently only with help from the higher science.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2476.summary: States the question of Article 4: whether theology is properly called wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2473.summary: Answers Article 4: theology is properly called wisdom.
claims: Theology is properly called wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2489.summary: Argument for the thesis: a habit to which all the conditions of wisdom properly belong is properly wisdom, and Aristotle's six conditions of the wise (Metaph. 1) all belong to theology: it knows all things (God and creatures, signs and things, per Lombard I d.1); it knows the most difficult things, to which our intellect is like the owl's eye to the sun; and it knows them most certainly, since it rests on infallible lights (faith in this life, glory in the next), its subject is the first truth, and its medium is the words of eternal truth.
claims: Theology satisfies Aristotle's conditions of wisdom.
Theology considers all things, the most difficult things, and knows them with certainty.
Theology's certainty rests on the infallible lights of faith and glory.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2569.summary: Anticipated objection: these considerations are not enough because of the disproportion between the knowable and the knower.
claims: The disproportion between God and our intellect undermines theology's certainty.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2578.summary: Reply: although the disproportion impedes the highest certainty of speculation in this life, it does not impede the highest certainty of firm adhesion, which in the true theologian is so great that he would die rather than dissent. The remaining conditions also fit: theology considers the cause of all causes; it exists not for other sciences but they for it; and it orders all other sciences and draws them into its service (Augustine). So Moses calls it true wisdom and understanding (Deut 4:6).
claims: Theology lacks the highest certainty of speculation but has the highest certainty of adhesion.
Theology considers the cause of causes, is sought for its own sake, and orders all other sciences.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2615.summary: Some agree that theology is properly wisdom but add two mistaken conditions: that it cannot be called science, and that it is not an adhesive habit since it causes no adhesion beyond that of faith. Thomas calls these additions useless and vain.
claims: Some hold that theology is wisdom but not science and not an adhesive habit.
These additions are mistaken.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2633.summary: Refutation of the first addition: Article 1 already refuted the claim that theology is not a science; moreover, since wisdom is 'savory science' (sapida scientia), calling a habit properly wisdom that is in no way science is a contradiction in terms.
claims: Wisdom is a kind of science, so a wisdom that is no science is a contradiction.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2651.summary: Introduces the arguments for the second addition, that theology is not an adhesive habit.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2660.summary: Arguments for the second addition: if theology produced adhesion beyond faith's, it would be opinion, which adheres imperfectly and with fear, and would thus infect rather than perfect the believer, who adheres firmly without fear. For the theologian adheres to his conclusions either as possibly otherwise (opinion) or as necessary (a deceptive habit, since he does not know them to be necessary). Moreover, the same intellect cannot adhere to the same truth in two ways at once, and the believer already adheres as to what cannot be otherwise.
claims: Additional adhesion from theology would be opinion, involving fear of error.
The same intellect cannot adhere to one truth in two ways at once.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2710.summary: Thomas rejects this: every intellectual habit that is properly wisdom attracts the mind and so produces adhesion to known truth; the opponents grant theology is properly wisdom; therefore it attracts the theologian and produces adhesion. The major is proved from Ethics 10: the activity of wisdom is the most delightful, and the delightful as such attracts and produces adhesion.
claims: Wisdom, being most delightful, attracts the mind and produces adhesion.
Theology, as wisdom, produces adhesion to theological truth.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2743.summary: Anticipated reply: Aristotle speaks of worldly wisdom, which our theology is not. Thomas answers that Aristotle speaks of all wisdom properly so called.
claims: Aristotle's claim about wisdom's delight applies to all wisdom properly so called.

HuYgTa-d1e304-d1e2764.summary: Further rebuttal: the opponent himself says theology is properly wisdom, and how can a theologian think human wisdom attracts and delights more than divine, when all Catholic writers say human wisdom illumines the intellect without inflaming the affect while divine wisdom illumines the intellect and inflames and refreshes the affect? Second, as in nature what removes indispositions conserves a form, so theology, by solving every objection against the articles, strengthens and causes adhesion. The opponents' first argument fails: fear (formido) is not of the essence of opinion (to be shown in the next question), and the theologian adheres to conclusions founded on truth that no human ingenuity can refute, an adhesion specifically different from faith's or opinion's, since faith, wisdom and opinion are three specifically different habits. Wisdom's adhesion is not repugnant to faith's. Finally, reply to the principal argument: though there is no single science of equivocals, there can be of analogicals, where one is attributed to another (Metaph. 4); theology's principal object is simply one, God, and all else is considered in relation to him.
claims: Divine wisdom, unlike human wisdom, both illumines the intellect and inflames the affect.
By solving objections, theology strengthens adhesion to the articles.
Formido is not of the essence of opinion.
Faith, wisdom and opinion cause specifically different adhesions.
There can be one science of analogicals, and theology's principal object, God, is simply one.

HuYgTa-d1e304-Dd1e452.summary: Article 4: whether theology is properly called wisdom. Thomas affirms that it is, since it fulfils all six of Aristotle's conditions of wisdom, having the highest certainty of adhesion though not of speculation. Against those who say theology is wisdom but neither science nor an adhesive habit, he argues that wisdom is 'savory science', that wisdom by its delight attracts and so produces adhesion — divine wisdom even more, since it inflames the affect — and that theology's adhesion is specifically distinct from that of faith and opinion. He closes the question by answering its principal argument: theology is one science of analogicals ordered to one God.
claims: Theology is properly wisdom.
Theology has the highest certainty of adhesion, not of speculation.
Theology is both science and wisdom and produces its own adhesion, distinct from faith's.
Theology is one science because its object is one, with all else considered by attribution to God.

HuYgTa-d1e304-Dd1e376.summary: Article 3: whether theology is a subalternate science. Following Giles of Rome, Thomas holds that theology is broadly subalternate, presupposing principles evident in God's and the blessed's science, but not properly, since the theologian cannot naturally attain that higher science. He defends the view that a subalternate science receives evidence of its principles from the subalternating one against a doctor who denies this, arguing that the doctor contradicts himself, and answers the doctor's three proofs by appealing to the lower science's operation by the higher's power.
claims: Theology is broadly but not properly subalternate.
A subalternate science has evidence of its principles only through the subalternating science.
By the higher science's power, a subalternate science can know and declare the causes of its principles.

HuYgTa-d1e304-Dd1e338.summary: Article 2: whether the articles of faith are the principles of theology. Thomas affirms that they are, since all of theology is regulated by them. He answers objections that theology proves, questions and defends the articles: metaphysics also proves its principles; theology, though special in subject, is the most common science in scope; it raises questions about the articles only to secure their correct application against heretics; and, like a subalternate science, it may hold its principles with less evidence than its conclusions. He then proves the thesis from the articles' functioning as rule and measure, as the object of greatest adhesion, as unprovable by anything prior, and as presupposed as most true.
claims: The articles of faith are theology's principles.
Theology inquires into the articles only regarding their application, not their truth.
Theology is special in subject but most common in scope.
A posteriori declaration of principles does not undermine their status as principles.
concepts: theology as special and common science

HuYgTa-d1e304-Dd1e206.summary: Article 1: whether theology is a science. Thomas holds that it is in some way a science but not strictly so. Against the strict-science view he argues that God has no cause and no adequate effect, rejects the posited supernatural 'light of theology' between faith and glory (it would weaken faith, could not be hidden, and is unnecessary for defending the faith), and refutes those who would derive articles like the Trinity from natural principles, which would destroy faith's merit. Against the no-science view, condemned at Paris in 1277, and its relatives — theology as knowledge of consequences only, as science in itself but not for us, or as three distinct habits — he argues for the inadequacy of each. His own conclusion is that theology proves properties of its subject (God as glorifier and ultimate end) with certainty comparable to moral science; demonstrations in the strict sense are rare even in philosophy, which is rife with disagreement, and theology can solve all objections to the faith by distinction or denial, as in the Trinitarian example of relative supposits.
claims: Theology is a science according to the capacity of the knower, not strictly as the knowable object would permit.
There is no special light of theology intermediate between faith and glory for doctors as a class.
The articles of faith cannot be derived from natural reason without destroying the merit of faith.
The view that theology is no science is condemned and erroneous.
Theology proves properties of its subject with certainty comparable to moral science.
All objections against the faith can be solved by distinction or interemptio.

HuYgTa-d1e304.summary: Prologue, Question 2: whether theology is a science. Across four articles Thomas argues that the theology of the wayfarer is truly a science — though according to the capacity of the knower rather than of the knowable — with the articles of faith as its principles; that it is broadly but not properly subalternate to the science of God and the blessed; and that it is properly wisdom. He rejects both the view that theology is science in the strict sense (including Henry of Ghent's special 'light of theology' and attempts to derive articles from natural reason) and the view that it is no science at all (condemned in 1277), along with intermediate views that make it a science of consequences only or split it into three habits. He answers the principal objection by holding that theology can be one science because its object, God, is one and all else is treated by attribution to him.
claims: The wayfarer's theology is truly a science, though according to the capacity of the knower.
The articles of faith are theology's principles.
Theology is broadly, not properly, subalternate to the science of God and the blessed.
Theology is properly called wisdom and produces its own kind of adhesion.
Theology is one science because its principal object is one and all else is considered in relation to it.
